newsitem.title: UK: Protestants echo US-British pleas for Irish peace.
newsitem.headline: Protestants echo US-British pleas for Irish peace.

text.p: Politicians linked to Protestant guerrillas on Wednesday urged them not to retaliate after an IRA bomb attack on a British army base that appeared to leave Northern Irish peace hopes in ruins.
The appeals echoed pleas by U.S. and British politicians who hope to avert a renewed outbreak of sectarian violence in the British-ruled province after two years of truce.

Politicians representing the Protestant majority said the Irish Republican Army had set a trap for so-called Loyalists with their double bomb blast at the British army's headquarters in Lisburn, south of Belfast on Monday.
The IRA admitted responsibility late on Tuesday.

"As always, we will be doing everything in our power...to see that the Loyalist ceasefire stays intact," said David Adams, a leader of the Ulster Democratic Party (UDP), the political wing of the banned Ulster Defence Association (UDA).
"But at the end of the day that decision, as always, rests with the Combined Loyalist Military Command (CLMC)," he said.
"We have to realise that Loyalists up until now have refused to be drawn back in. Let's hope they realise yet again that that is what (IRA) republicans want... and that they refuse to do it."
In Washington a statement from the White House condemned the IRA action that injured 31 people, as "a barbaric act".
Anthony Lake, President Clinton's national security adviser, said that if Loyalists rejoined the conflict "it could destroy the future of Northern Ireland".
British Prime Minister John Major also appealed for calm following the IRA attack. The IRA seeks to oust Britain from Northern Ireland and unite the divided island.
"The Provisional IRA are trying to provoke a general return to violence in Northern Ireland. We must not let them succeed. I appeal to all Loyalists not to fall into this trap," Major said.

The attack, at the heart of Britain's military presence in the province, was the IRA's first attack in the region since ditching a ceasefire in February with bombs confined to the British mainland, and one at a British army camp in Germany.
Loyalists stopped their campaign against Catholics in October 1994 and have kept to their ceasefire.

Media reports said that outlawed groups in the CLMC, the umbrella organisation that controlled an onslaught on the Irish nationalist Catholic minority for 25 years, met individually on Tuesday. They said the CLMC would meet shortly to consider strategy in the light of the IRA's admission of responsibility for the Lisburn bomb.
The IRA bomb and the possibility of a CLMC back-to-war move have raised tensions among Catholics and Protestants alike.

"We should avoid as best we can the cycle of violence that undoubtedly would take us to hell and back again," David Ervine of the Progressive Unionist Party (PUP), the political wing of the banned Ulster Volunteer Force, told Reuters.

The IRA attack followed fresh statements by Britain and Ireland that the IRA's political wing, Sinn Fein, would not be allowed to join peace talks in Belfast until the IRA renewed its ceasefire and signed up to principles of non-violence.

The talks group pro-British Unionists and the Irish nationalist Social Democratic and Labour party of John Hume but the absence of Sinn Fein means the guerrillas whose war is at the heart of the conflict are not represented.

"Sinn Fein have excluded themselves more clearly than ever," Major told reporters, soon after Sinn Fein president Gerry Adams said he was willing to hold talks with the British government at a moment's notice.
